steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing TRACE-GPT, a generative pre-trained Transformer model for unsupervised fault detection on time-series sensor data in semiconductor manufacturing. Explain the industrial problem and its challenges, review why existing FDC, representation, classification and anomaly detection approaches fall short, motivate generative pre-training, and list contributions and the paper structure.

  - recent unsupervised fault classification (cite) still tunes anomaly detection hyperparameters via fault detection stages, partly supervised
  - time-series representation: TS-TCC (cite), TST (cite), TS2Vec (cite); classification, anomaly detection, forecasting; but classifiers via supervised methods e.g. SVM
  - RTFN (cite): unsupervised clustering but must be embedded in supervised structure for classification features
  - MDAN (cite): time + frequency domain features; needs much data for transfer learning source->target; only electrocardiogram or motion sensor data

  - humans discern anomalies models struggle with

  - generative pre-training helps with unlabeled data (cite), improves image tasks (cite)
  - Transformer (cite) -> GPT (cite) outperformed most state-of-the-art NLP benchmarks (cite)

  - Time-series Anomaly-detection with Convolutional Embedding and Generative Pre-trained Transformers
  - Transformer decoder + temporal convolutional networks learn sequential features of sensor data

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Even now, even in a leading semiconductor company, equipment engineers check process logs with their own eyes every day to see whether they are normal or not. To reduce and automate this inefficiency, there has been research on Fault Detection and Classification (FDC), time-series classification, and time-series anomaly detection. These research areas are closely connected as shown in Fig. I.

Despite all this research, the semiconductor manufacturing industry still faces this inefficiency because of the following challenges:

- • First, there is a lack of abnormal data. Abnormal data may not have been obtained in sufficient amounts at the time the detection model is developed. The goal of the semiconductor manufacturing industry is to minimize defects, so the datasets it handles are highly biased with scarce anomalies. Often models have to be developed that can detect future anomalies even without any abnormal data. In this case many supervised machine learning methods, like convolutional neural networks (CNN) or K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), cannot be applied.

- • Second, data itself is scarce. Previous time-series studies usually had training data with sample sizes in the double digits. But because rapid circuit integration technology is advancing faster, in the semiconductor industry, where development timelines are crucial, model development often has to start with only a handful of available data. In these circumstances labeled data is even harder to get, so unsupervised learning is essential. Precise data labeling especially requires extensive inspection or measurement steps before and after the process, which increases costs. This conflicts with the fact that fault detection in semiconductor manufacturing is done to maximize productivity and profits.

- • Last, together with the challenges above, there are various mixed types of normal time-series data, which makes the problem even more complex. For example, semiconductor manufacturing processes need the process conditions to be adjusted continuously. So the definition of a normal time-series can vary. Datasets can therefore contain mixed types of normality, and this makes it impossible to use traditional algorithms like dynamic time warping (DTW).

- Existing work
  - FDC-CNN: supervised, high accuracy, but labels costly; recent unsupervised fault classification still partly supervised
  - representation (TS-TCC, TST, TS2Vec): classifiers still supervised (SVM)
  - RTFN: needs supervised structure; MDAN: needs much data, only electrocardiogram / motion sensor data
  - our setting: limited data, mixed sensors (gas, electric, pressure, light emission)
  - unsupervised anomaly detection (Fig. I): varied-length subsequences, single or collective points; still hard on real data
- Motivation: humans spot anomalies; generative pre-training; Transformer -> GPT
- TRACE-GPT: Transformer decoder + temporal convolutional networks
  - contributions: architecture; modified Transformer predicting next sensor values; evaluation on extreme datasets
- Structure: Sections II to VI

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Even now, even in a leading semiconductor company, equipment engineers check process logs with their own eyes every day to see whether they are normal or not. To reduce and automate this inefficiency, there has been research on Fault Detection and Classification (FDC), time-series classification, and time-series anomaly detection. These research areas are closely connected as shown in Fig. I.

Despite all this research, the semiconductor manufacturing industry still faces this inefficiency because of the following challenges:

- • First, there is a lack of abnormal data. Abnormal data may not have been obtained in sufficient amounts at the time the detection model is developed. The goal of the semiconductor manufacturing industry is to minimize defects, so the datasets it handles are highly biased with scarce anomalies. Often models have to be developed that can detect future anomalies even without any abnormal data. In this case many supervised machine learning methods, like convolutional neural networks (CNN) or K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), cannot be applied.

- • Second, data itself is scarce. Previous time-series studies usually had training data with sample sizes in the double digits. But because rapid circuit integration technology is advancing faster, in the semiconductor industry, where development timelines are crucial, model development often has to start with only a handful of available data. In these circumstances labeled data is even harder to get, so unsupervised learning is essential. Precise data labeling especially requires extensive inspection or measurement steps before and after the process, which increases costs. This conflicts with the fact that fault detection in semiconductor manufacturing is done to maximize productivity and profits.

- • Last, together with the challenges above, there are various mixed types of normal time-series data, which makes the problem even more complex. For example, semiconductor manufacturing processes need the process conditions to be adjusted continuously. So the definition of a normal time-series can vary. Datasets can therefore contain mixed types of normality, and this makes it impossible to use traditional algorithms like dynamic time warping (DTW).

One of the most common methods in the semiconductor manufacturing industry today is using CNNs, like FDC-CNN, to classify normal and abnormal data with supervised learning. They combined feature engineering techniques and supervised learning algorithms and got high accuracy in fault detection and classification. It performs well when it can be applied, but in the real world there are many cases where it cannot be used because building labeled data is so expensive. In unsupervised learning, even the most recent research that tries unsupervised fault classification on manufacturing data has the limitation that the hyperparameters of the anomaly detection model have to be fine-tuned through the fault detection stages, so it partly uses a supervised approach.

In many fields, not only the semiconductor manufacturing industry, time-series representation is a prominent domain that explores the characteristics of time-series data with unsupervised learning. Recently TS-TCC, TST, and TS2Vec tried to develop unsupervised representation techniques for time-series data that can be used for tasks like classification, anomaly detection, and forecasting. But the limitation of unsupervised representation approaches is that they rely on supervised learning methods, like Support Vector Machines (SVM), to build classifiers.

The Robust Temporal Feature Network (RTFN) looks at a deep learning approach to the challenge of developing unsupervised time-series classification models. But RTFN can do unsupervised clustering, and still in the end it has to be embedded into a supervised structure to extract features for classification. More recently a model called the Multimodal Domain Adversarial Network (MDAN) showed promising performance in time-series classification by using both time-domain and frequency-domain feature representations. But MDAN needs a lot of data during training for transfer learning from source to target data, and it was only studied on electrocardiogram or motion sensor data. Our study instead aims to address issues in semiconductor manufacturing processes where only limited data is given or where various sensors like gas, electric, pressure, and light emission are mixed.

Unsupervised time-series anomaly detection methods can be used to achieve end-to-end unsupervised classification as shown in Fig. I. Time-series anomaly detection methods can find anomalous subsequences of different lengths within time-series, which can be a single point or collective points. Still, solving real-world problems is hard. Our study shows the limitations of existing unsupervised time-series anomaly detection methods on datasets from the semiconductor manufacturing industry.

Humans can relatively easily spot anomalies that existing models struggle with, despite the challenges mentioned above. A key motivation of this research is that a certain type of deep learning model can detect infinite kinds of potential anomalies of time-series data in semiconductor manufacturing. In other domains like image processing or Natural Language Processing (NLP), generative pre-training has also been proposed to help deep learning with unlabeled data, and it has been used to improve performance on image processing tasks. After the Transformer model was suggested, Transformer based models like Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT) were developed and outperformed most state-of-the-art benchmarks in NLP tasks.

In this paper we introduce a new deep learning architecture, TRACE-GPT: Time-seRies Anomaly-detection with Convolutional Embedding and Generative Pre-trained Transformers. We show that the Transformer decoder can learn sequential features of semiconductor manufacturing sensor data effectively with temporal convolutional networks. The key contributions of this paper are:

- • We propose a new deep learning architecture, TRACE-GPT, for unsupervised time-series anomaly detection in semiconductor manufacturing. We also developed a model that can classify abnormal data by observing unlabeled data, like a human, without any prior knowledge of anomalies or possible anomalies.

- • We introduce a modified version of the Transformer architecture, which was originally designed for natural language processing, so that it handles time-series data effectively. The Transformer architecture's idea is to predict the next words in a sentence, and we extended it to learn from numerical sequences and predict the next sensor values.

- • Considering the real-world challenges in the semiconductor manufacturing industry, we evaluated our model on extreme datasets, with scenarios like insufficient abnormal data, single-digit-sized training data, unlabeled data, or mixed normal types. We showed that our model outperforms other baselines.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the related works for this study. Section III describes the architecture and methodology of our deep learning model. Section IV explains the datasets from the semiconductor manufacturing industry we did experiments on. Section V discusses the experimental setup and the results on these datasets. Section VI summarizes how we achieved the motivation of our research.

steps.text:
Even at this moment, even in a leading semiconductor company, equipment engineers verify process logs with their own eyes on a daily basis to see whether they are normal or not. To reduce and automate this inefficiency, research on Fault Detection and Classification (FDC) [1,2,3,4,5], time-series classification [6,7,8], and time-series anomaly detection [9,10,11,12] has been conducted. These research areas are closely interconnected, as shown in Fig. I.

Despite extensive research efforts, the semiconductor manufacturing industry still faces this inefficiency due to the following challenges:

- • First, the lack of abnormal data is a challenge: abnormal data may not have been sufficiently obtained when the detection model is developed. The semiconductor manufacturing industry aims to minimize defects, which leads to highly biased datasets with scarce anomalies [13]. It is often necessary to develop models that can detect future anomalies without any abnormal data. In this case, many supervised machine learning methods, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN) [1] or K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) [14], become inapplicable.

- • Second, the scarcity of data itself is a challenge. Previous studies in time series typically used training data with sample sizes in the double digits [15]. However, with accelerated advancements in rapid circuit integration technology, in the semiconductor industry, where development timelines are crucial, model development often has to begin with only a handful of available data. Under these circumstances, labeled data becomes even harder to acquire, making unsupervised learning essential [16]. Precise data labeling in particular requires extensive inspection or measurement steps before and after the process, increasing costs. This conflicts with the fact that fault detection in semiconductor manufacturing is conducted to maximize productivity and profits [17].

- • Last, in conjunction with the challenges above, the presence of various mixed types of normal time-series data makes the problem even more complex. For instance, semiconductor manufacturing processes require continuous adjustment of the process conditions [18], so the definition of a normal time-series can vary. Consequently, datasets can contain mixed types of normality, which makes traditional algorithms such as dynamic time warping (DTW) [19] impossible to use.

Fig. I: An illustration of fault detection and classification using time-series anomaly detection in the semiconductor manufacturing industry, showing the relationship between fault, anomaly, and abnormal wafer, as well as the stages of anomaly detection and classification.

One of the most commonly used methods in the semiconductor manufacturing industry today is to use CNNs, such as FDC-CNN [1], to classify normal and abnormal data through supervised learning. Its authors combined feature engineering techniques with supervised learning algorithms to achieve high accuracy in fault detection and classification. Although it performs well when applicable, there are many real-world cases where it cannot be used because of the high cost of building labeled data. In unsupervised learning, even the most recent research [5] attempting unsupervised fault classification on manufacturing data is limited by having to fine-tune the hyperparameters of the anomaly detection model through the fault detection stages, partially relying on a supervised approach.

Across various fields, not only semiconductor manufacturing, a prominent domain that explores the characteristics of time-series data through unsupervised learning is time-series representation. Recently, TS-TCC [20], TST [21], and TS2Vec [22] aimed to develop unsupervised representation techniques for time-series data that could be used for tasks such as classification, anomaly detection, and forecasting. Nevertheless, unsupervised representation approaches are limited in that they rely on supervised learning methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), to construct classifiers.

To tackle the challenge of developing unsupervised time-series classification models, the Robust Temporal Feature Network (RTFN) investigates a deep learning approach [6]. However, although RTFN can perform unsupervised clustering, it ultimately needs to be embedded into a supervised structure to extract features for classification. More recently, the Multimodal Domain Adversarial Network (MDAN) has shown promising performance in time-series classification by incorporating both time-domain and frequency-domain feature representations [8]. However, MDAN requires a substantial amount of data during training for transfer learning from source to target data, and it has been studied only on electrocardiogram or motion sensor data. In contrast, our study addresses issues in semiconductor manufacturing processes where only limited data is provided or where a mix of sensors such as gas, electric, pressure, and light emission is present.

To achieve end-to-end unsupervised classification as shown in Fig. I, unsupervised time-series anomaly detection methods can be used. These methods can find anomalous subsequences of varied lengths within time-series, which can be either single points or collective points [11]. Nonetheless, solving real-world problems remains challenging, and our study shows the limitations of existing unsupervised time-series anomaly detection methods on datasets from the semiconductor manufacturing industry.

Despite the challenges mentioned earlier, humans can relatively easily discern anomalies that existing models struggle with. A key motivation of this research is that a certain type of deep learning model can detect infinite kinds of potential anomalies of time-series data in semiconductor manufacturing. In other domains such as image processing and Natural Language Processing (NLP), generative pre-training has also been proposed to help deep learning with unlabeled data [23] and used to improve performance on image processing tasks [24]. After the Transformer model was proposed [25], Transformer based models such as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT) [26] were developed and outperformed most state-of-the-art benchmarks in NLP tasks [27,28,29].

In this paper, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture, TRACE-GPT: Time-seRies Anomaly-detection with Convolutional Embedding and Generative Pre-trained Transformers. We demonstrate that the Transformer decoder, combined with temporal convolutional networks, can effectively learn sequential features of semiconductor manufacturing sensor data. The key contributions of this paper are as follows:

- • We propose a novel deep learning architecture, TRACE-GPT, for unsupervised time-series anomaly detection in semiconductor manufacturing. We further developed a model that can classify abnormal data by observing unlabeled data, like a human, without any prior knowledge of anomalies or possible anomalies.

- • We introduce a modified version of the Transformer architecture, originally designed for natural language processing, to handle time-series data effectively. The Transformer architecture is designed to predict the next words in a sentence; we extended it to learn from numerical sequences and predict the next sensor values.

- • Considering the real-world challenges of the semiconductor manufacturing industry, we evaluated our model on extreme datasets covering the following scenarios: insufficient abnormal data, single-digit-sized training data, unlabeled data, or mixed normal types. We demonstrated that our model outperforms other baselines.

The structure of this paper is as follows: Section II introduces related works. Section III describes the architecture and methodology of the proposed deep learning model. Section IV explains in detail the datasets from the semiconductor manufacturing industry used in our experiments. Section V describes the experimental setup and presents the results on these datasets. Finally, Section VI summarizes how we achieved the motivation of our research.
